A user ran a script on BigQuery against historical HTTP Archive public data and was billed $14,000 by Google Cloud 'with zero warning whatsoever.' Google would not remove the fee, and the user said there is 'basically zero customer support.'

The $14k bill came from a script that ran one query per month back to 2016 for each of several sites. The user had done this before without issues. It ran for 2 hours, and the first notice was the credit card charge.

The console shows 'TBs scanned' in very small letters before you press go. On on-demand billing you can multiply that by $6.25 to get the exact query cost. The commenter called it 'a design that's hostile to new customers... But it is comprehensible.'

Complaint that Google hides query cost behind the abstract 'TBs scanned' metric (in a non-open format that is hard to estimate) or 'slots'. The commenter said most people only learn how this works after an unexpected bill, and wants the dollar cost shown directly in the console and API.

Counterpoint: 'I've worked with much larger datasets on BQ (petabyte scale) and managed to not spend more than $1000 in an hour.' BQ tells you how much data will be processed BEFORE you run the query, which makes cost implications easier to understand.

Workaround: you can set a byte-size limit for individual queries plus custom quotas. Caveat: a script looping a 49 GiB query 1000 times still bypasses a 50 GiB per-query limit, so batch processes need careful cost design.
Cost is driven by data scanned, not logic. 'Select * is dangerous because it's a column store.' Look at the schema, select only the columns you need, and filter on partitions/clusters.

Praise despite the cost complaints: BigQuery is 'a publicly-accessible data supercomputer' that 'can move some serious data.' The commenter credits Google for making such power available to anyone with a credit card, while agreeing cost transparency is lacking.

Hands-on review after a week with BigQuery pipe syntax: 'way more productive than just SQL' for exploration and cleaning. It unifies WHERE/HAVING/QUALIFY and makes iterating on arrays and parsing JSON much better. It's great for DBT macros, and the BQ console completions do 'an okay job.' Downsides: no typing helpers, the reader must track state through many steps, and it is less portable.

BigQuery already has table-valued functions, which can be used with pipe syntax via a CALL clause. Another commenter showed a CREATE TEMP TABLE FUNCTION built from pipe operators and reused with |> CALL.
Annual flat-rate plan is going from 2.3c to 4.8c per slot hour, and on-demand pricing is rising 25% ($5/TB to $6.25/TB). 'Seems like they are trying to squeeze the users who are most locked in.'

Storage gets cheaper under the new pricing, but 'in our case, compute makes up more than 80% of costs, even though we store a large amount of data. I suspect most big customers will come out much worse from this.'
On lock-in: 'Migrating off of BigQuery would likely take months for any decent sized deployment.'

Comparison: when this user ran large-scale queries on AWS Athena, it was 'like two orders of magnitude slower than BigQuery for the same queries.' The UI, docs and UX were 'nowhere near as good as BigQuery's... it's genuinely a good product.'

Athena on S3 is similar to BQ external tables, but 'BQ is much faster' and Athena gets more expensive on large datasets. Another commenter: 'BigQuery is much, much better than Redshift,' though both are worse than Snowflake.
At a previous job, BigQuery was the only Google Cloud service used; everything else was on AWS. Another user said their company was the same.

'Bigquery is one of the tools i've been most impressed with the last 20 years. It just works so much faster than I assumed it would.' The commenter expects the price hike to push some users to self-host OSS alternatives.
Former user: 'I enjoyed that you only paid for data read. It was such a simple way to think about it.' A reply notes that at larger scale, dedicated slot reservations are much cheaper than on-demand.
Tested the BigQuery-Sheets connector for their org: 'there's a lot of promise.' The only criticism is that formulas created in the query come back as Text cells. Workaround: cast them as Automatic.
Complaint that it was still hard to get a Google CloudSQL DB into BigQuery; the team used a third-party service to copy data from CloudSQL to BigQuery.
